Chapter 2: Sorting the Impossible — How Physics Classifies What Can and Can’t Be Done
Imagine you’re sitting around a table with friends, tossing around wild ideas. Someone wonders if humans will ever teleport. Another jokes about buying an invisibility cloak at the mall. There’s laughter, a little skepticism, and maybe even some hope mixed in. Some folks swear that science fiction is just science waiting to happen, while others are sure there are limits we’ll never cross.
But here’s something most people never think about—physicists actually have their own way of answering these questions. They don’t just say “never” or “maybe someday.” Instead, there’s this quiet system they use, a kind of mental sorting hat for the impossible. They look at each wild idea and ask, “Does this fit with what we know about the universe?” It’s not about closing doors—it’s about knowing which ones might open, and which are locked by the laws of nature themselves.
The real heart of this system is the idea that “impossible” isn’t always as final as it sounds. Sometimes, something seems impossible just because our technology hasn’t caught up yet. Other times, it runs smack into the deepest rules of physics. And then—there are those tempting ideas that hover in the gray area, just out of reach.
Let’s break it down. The first group physicists talk about is called Class I impossibilities. These are things that sound wild now, but they don’t actually violate any laws we know of. They might just need another century—or a big leap in our understanding. Take invisibility cloaks. Believe it or not, scientists are already tinkering with materials that can bend light in strange ways, making objects almost vanish. Or think about ray guns and energy shields. They’re still science fiction, but the science behind them isn’t completely out of left field.
Then there’s a second group— Class II impossibilities. These are ideas that don’t break the rules, but would need breakthroughs so massive, they could be thousands or even millions of years away. Time machines and traveling faster than light fall into this camp. The equations don’t scream “impossible”—but the challenges feel almost insurmountable. Imagine staring up at a mountain whose peak is lost in the clouds. You know it’s up there, but getting there? That’s another story.
And finally, we have the “brick wall” cases— Class III impossibilities. These dreams run straight into the hard limits of physics as we know it. Like perpetual motion machines, which would need to create energy out of thin air. That breaks the rule that energy can’t just appear out of nowhere. These aren’t just tough—they flat-out clash with the universe’s playbook.
But even here, physicists stay humble. History is full of moments when the “impossible” became reality. The limits of physics aren’t set in stone—they grow and shift with every new discovery. So, what seems out of reach today? With the right flash of insight, it just might become tomorrow’s breakthrough.
